sentences.text: From question to publication with Remote Data Collection: webcam eye tracking and facial expressions online
This workshop follows one advertising question from a client's first sentence to a written results and discussion section, for a study that runs entirely online.

You will plan a test of two food waste videos and an infographic, build it in iMotions Lab 11 point 1 as a Remote Data Collection (R D C) study, send it out by link, let respondents take part at home on their own computers, bring the data back to the lab computer, score the faces, test three hypotheses, and write the result for a journal and a client.
Every section explains why before how.
In a remote study the respondent's own computer is the lab.
The study opens in a web browser from a collect link, and the webcam does the measuring.

Webcam eye tracking estimates where on the screen a person looks, after a calibration, a sequence of dots the respondent follows with the eyes so that the software can map that person's eyes onto the screen.

Webcam facial expression analysis scores the recorded face with Affectiva aff decks, which estimates "the probability that a trained human coder would rate that action unit/emotion as present," on a scale out of 100.
iMotions offers two routes.

iMotions Online is "a fully browser-based experimental platform": the study is built, run, analyzed, and exported at my dot imotions dot com, the iMotions web portal, and "Eye tracking and facial expression data are processed on iMotions' servers based in Denmark (Copenhagen)."
The researcher never handles the face video.

R D C "is integrated with iMotions Lab software for analysis": the study is built in Lab, uploaded to my dot imotions dot com, which "provides a website link for study participation," and brought back as a study zip file loaded into Lab.

For a remote study built in Lab, the face scores come only from post processing on the lab computer (Post Processing, then Affectiva) after that download, because iMotions deprecated remote batch processing on June 1, 2026 and the Sensors switches on my dot imotions dot com are locked for such studies.
In return, every Lab tool applies, from the thresholding notebooks to areas of interest.
This workshop teaches both routes and uses R D C for the worked example.
The single most important idea: a remote study trades control for reach.
Eye tracking error is measured in degrees of visual angle, the angle at the eye between where a person looked and where the tracker placed the gaze.

For webcam data the iMotions Online Study Setup guide calls under 1 degree excellent, 0 to 4 degrees generally acceptable, and above 5 degrees unreliable (two other iMotions Online articles recommend a threshold of 3.0 degrees; section 06 sets the two side by side), and iMotions says its algorithm "does not have the sub-degree accuracy of a conventional infrared eye tracker"; Smart Eye's white paper for the lab's Aurora reports a median error of about 0.54 degrees.
A webcam can show which large region of a screen drew the eyes, never which word.
Faces change less, since the lab's own respondent camera is also a webcam, but at home nobody controls the light, the distance, the device, or who walks past.
The real work is the data quality plan written before collection.

The lab has had iMotions Online since May 22, 2026 (first a trial for 30 respondents) and R D C with webcam eye tracking since June 2026, uploaded only from the computer holding license key 0001 (Lab Alien).
The Prolific integration is not enabled for the lab's account, and J S U has no Qualtrics license.
The lab has run one remote study for a campus client; its lessons are in the lab's fix checklist (Project doc 13).
The worked example is the vendor demo (DEMO) Food Waste webET FEA voice, with a simulated data set of 260 sessions.
Time needed.
About 5 hours over two sittings: sections 01 to 05 (planning, building, collecting) in the first, 06 to 10 (data, analysis, and writing) in the second
Equipment.
The lab computer with license key 0001 (Lab Alien) for building, uploading, and post processing, and a second computer with a webcam to test the link as a respondent
SoftwareiMotions Lab 11 point 1 with Affectiva aff decks and cloud upload (key 0001), a my dot imotions dot com login, and R or Excel for section 08
Data files.

The simulated remote study files in the site's data folder (session data, quality table, F E A and A O I exports, survey, analysis dot R, Excel workbook), plus (DEMO) Food Waste webET FEA voice in the lab Library
How to use.
Work top to bottom, answer each quick check, then tick the section
You need this page and, for sections 04, 05, and 07, the lab computer and a my dot imotions dot com login, but no earlier workshop.
If you did Workshop 2 (eye tracking in the lab) or Workshop 3 (facial expression in the lab), you will recognize areas of interest and thresholding; nothing here depends on them.
The statistics you need are a mean, a standard deviation (how far a typical value sits from the mean), and the idea that a test asks whether a difference is larger than chance would produce.
Terms with a dotted underline open a definition when you tap them.
Help center links open after you sign in through my dot imotions dot com; for a longer introduction, read Getting Started with Remote Data Collection (R D C).
Nothing in this workshop changes the lab's existing studies or starts collection on a live study.
Open (DEMO) Food Waste webET FEA voice only to look, cancel any processing dialog it opens, and do not play a respondent's camera recording.
The one sentence this workshop keeps repeating Write the exclusion rule and the consent text before the first link goes out.

Once collection has started, the study and its stimuli can no longer be changed (iMotions pages put the lock at the first respondent's data or at the first accepted consent), and an R D C study's consent text locks "once the first respondent accepts the consent form."
A rule written after seeing the data is a rule chosen to get a result, and a consent screen that does not say what the webcam records cannot be repaired for the people who have already agreed to it.

Say what a remote biometric study is, tell iMotions Online from R D C and where each computes the face scores, explain why a webcam supports large screen regions and not words, and list the lab's licenses, equipment, software, and files for this workshop.
From idea to research question
A client rarely arrives with a research question, only a business question.

Picture an organization that campaigns against food waste (a teaching scenario modeled on the iMotions demo study, not a real client) that asks: "Which of our two food waste videos moves people more, and which tip on our infographic do they read?"
The sentence names two videos and two wishes, but not who will watch, what "moves" means, how it will be measured, or what difference would count.
A research question names the problem the study will answer and signals the kind of study needed; a hypothesis is a testable answer to it, written with the variables that will be measured.
"Moves" first.
aff decks does not read feelings; it estimates, frame by frame, the probability that a trained coder would rate an expression as present.

Its Engagement score is derived from a combination of facial movements and describes how expressive the face is, not attention to the message or persuasion; valence says whether an expression looks pleasant or unpleasant.

F E A thresholding, an iMotions analysis notebook, marks every moment a score is above a cutoff (50 in the vendor's analysis of this demo), which turns each video into a percent of time score, such as the share of the video during which Engagement was above 50.
"Moves people more" can become "keeps faces expressive for a larger share of the video," a narrower claim.
Then "read."
Webcam eye tracking can say which large region drew the eyes, and for how long.

An area of interest (A O I) is a region drawn on a stimulus; dwell time is the total time the gaze rested inside it, summed over fixations, the pauses in which the eyes hold still; and time to first fixation (T T F F) is how long the first fixation took to land there.
Because a webcam's error is a few degrees of visual angle, an A O I the size of a tip box works and one the size of a word does not.
"Which tip do they read" can become "which of four tip boxes draws the most dwell time," which says where the eyes rested, not whether the words were read or understood.
What a webcam study can answerWas the visual video met with expressive faces (Engagement above 50) for a larger share of its running time than the narrative video, in the same respondents?
Which of four large tip boxes drew the most dwell time, and in what order were they first fixated?
At which step did the people who opened the link stop, and did that depend on the order of the videos?
What it cannot answerWhich word or line did a respondent read?
Did viewers feel guilt, disgust, or hope?
Will they waste less food next month?
Who else was in the room?
Each needs another measure: a lab eye tracker for small text, self report for feelings, a behavioral criterion for waste.
Why run the study remotely at all?
Reach: the lab's decision guide chooses a remote study when people are off campus or more than about 60 are needed quickly.
A natural setting: respondents watch on their own screens at home.
Cost: no lab session to schedule for each person.
The price is control.

Nobody sets the light, the distance, or the device, or sees whether the respondent talks, slumps, or leaves; webcam tracking is "sensitive to talking, head movement, and the use of glasses," and iMotions advises over-recruiting because biosensor data are "much more variable when collected remotely."
Only people with a computer and a webcam who agree to be filmed at home take part, which is called self selection, and some who start will stop, which is called attrition.
Is a face recorded over the internet worth measuring?
Advertising researchers have used such faces: to measure ad preferences automatically from facial responses gathered over the Internet (McDuff and colleagues
, 2014), to predict ad liking and purchase intent in a large-scale analysis of facial responses to ads, to study emotion-induced engagement in Internet video advertisements (Teixeira and colleagues
, 2012), and to ask, in a web-based facial tracking field study, why, when, and how much ads should entertain.
The word engagement in one of those titles need not mean aff decks Engagement, so a report always says which engagement it means.
Webcam eye tracking has a literature of its own: WebGazer, scalable webcam eye tracking using user interactions (Papoutsaki and colleagues

, 2016); a first look at online webcam-based eye tracking in cognitive science; webcam-based online eye tracking for behavioral research; comparisons of webcam and remote eye tracking (Wisiecka and colleagues

, 2022), of online webcam and laboratory eye tracking with infants, and of a new webcam-based system with the EyeLink 1000, under a title that calls the result "close to laboratory standards" (Kaduk and colleagues
, 2024); a web-based replication of an earlier visual world experiment using WebGazer.js; and deep learning models for webcam eye tracking in online experiments.

They differ in algorithm, screen, and task, so no number from them can stand in for the accuracy of iMotions web E T 3.0, the algorithm the portal names; iMotions lists a web E T 3.0 validation among its science resources, to be read in its final form before anyone quotes it.

The vendor's analysis of the demo suggests a direction: with thresholding at 50, "The Visual video had higher levels of engagement (57 percent time spent) compared to the Narrative video (19 percent time spent)."
The article does not say how many respondents that analysis used (the lab copy holds four), so it is motivation, not evidence: a plan may borrow its direction, never its numbers.
Now the hypotheses, written before any data exist.
The video is compared within subjects, each respondent with himself or herself, because everyone sees both; the order, which video comes first, differs between respondents and is set by chance.
The percent of time Engaged (aff decks Engagement above 50) is higher during foodwaste visual than during foodwaste narrative, within the same respondents.
Dwell time on the infographic differs among its four tip A O I's.
Intention to reduce food waste (one survey item, 1 to 7) does not differ between respondents who saw the narrative video first and those who saw the visual video first: a randomization check.
Quality analyses, planned in advance.

Where sessions stopped; completion by order; exclusions by reason; the change in calibration accuracy from the first to the last calibration; accuracy and hits on the smallest A O I; and the tests repeated under a stricter threshold.
Exploratory.
Whether the Engagement difference goes with naming the visual video more persuasive, and whether dwell time on the tips goes with the number of tips recalled.
Every test can detect a difference in either direction, but a hypothesis may state one when a reason is written down first.
H 1 does, because the visual video was made with "provocative visual imagery" and the vendor's analysis pointed the same way; it is supported only if significant in that direction.
H 2 does not: the tips differ in content and in position, and nothing known beforehand says which should win.
H 3 is not a test of the videos at all.
Everyone answers after seeing both, so the order groups differ only in which video came first, and chance decided that.
If the split worked and order does not matter, intention should be about the same in both groups; a difference would point to an order effect or to a split that was not random.
A nonsignificant randomization check is reassurance, not proof that the groups are equal.
Now the client's sentence can be rewritten.
The lab's decision guide asks every study for one sentence with four slots: who, sees what, measured how, compared against what.

Here: adults with a computer and a webcam who open a study link (who) watch both videos, in an order set by chance, and then the infographic (sees what), while the webcam records the face for aff decks and estimates gaze after a calibration (measured how), and each respondent's two videos are compared with each other and the four tips with each other (against what).
Weak questions fail in their own ways.
"Which video works?"
asks for a judgment; "Which video do people love?"
asks about feeling; "Which tip do they agree with?"
asks about attitude; "Which sentence do they read?"
asks for an accuracy a webcam does not have.
The repair names an observable, a window, and a comparison, and it claims more expressive faces and longer looks, not more persuasion and not more reading.
The last step is to choose one primary measure per hypothesis before the data exist.
aff decks produces dozens of signals (the iMotions Online list holds 39), and every A O I has twelve fixation based metrics; test them all and something will come out by chance.
Here the primary measures are the percent of time Engaged for H 1, dwell time on the four tips for H 2, and the intention item for H 3.
Joy, Brow Furrow, valence, and T T F F are described, not tested, and the quality analyses are reported whatever the hypotheses show.

Turn a client's question about moving people and reading into testable questions, say what webcam eye tracking and webcam facial expression analysis can and cannot support, weigh what a remote study gains and loses, and write three hypotheses, one of them a randomization check, with one primary measure each.
Designing a remote study
A remote study is designed around three facts.
People differ a great deal in how expressive their faces are.
Webcam eye tracking is off by a few degrees, and it gets worse as a session goes on.
And many people who open the link will not finish.
Each fact shapes one part of the plan.
The videos are compared within subjects: every respondent sees both, so a respondent's general expressiveness enters both scores and drops out of the difference.
The cost is order, because the second video is watched by someone who has just seen the first.
Counterbalancing uses both orders, and randomization, assignment by chance, decides who gets which.
The demo randomized its video order; one way to do that in iMotions Lab is a block whose display order is random.
This plan instead makes each order its own study flow, a separate path through the stimuli (Study flow 1, narrative first; Study flow 2, visual first).

The portal's respondent list names each session's flow in its Block column, and the plan assumes it does so even for sessions that stop before the videos (modeled), so completion can be compared by order.

A 2024 manual screenshot shows one LINK per BLOCK for an R D C study, so each flow gets its own collect link, and the invitation list is split at random into two halves, one link each (modeled; verify on the lab computer that an R D C study built in Lab 11 point 1 can do this).
Next, the infographic.
Its A O I size, the area of an A O I in square pixels or percent of the screen, must fit the tracker's error.

R D C fixes the screen settings of every study at 1920 by 1080 pixels on a screen 47.4 by 29.6 cm seen from 65 cm, and a calculation from those settings puts one degree of visual angle at about 46 pixels across the screen, so an error of 3 degrees can move a gaze point about 140 pixels.

The iMotions Online introduction advises that "it is best to create large objects that have a buffer of space between them," and the iMotions A O I article, which cites a recommendation of about 1 to 1.5 degrees of padding around an A O I, adds that "webcam eye tracking requires an even greater buffer."

The plan therefore draws four equal tip boxes (262400 square pixels, 12.65 percent of the screen each) and a wide, thin Headline banner (176000 square pixels, 8.49 percent), with gaps between them so that an error near an edge does not land in a neighbor.
Calibration is also where the error is measured.
Accuracy is "the mean distance between the actual and expected gaze positions calculated during calibration," in degrees, so smaller is better.

Every R D C study gets a 13 point Pre-study calibration and Post-study calibration by default (39 seconds each in the Lab stimulus bar), and the R D C webcam article calls this bookending "currently the best practice that we recommend for webcam eye tracking."

The reason is calibration drift, the worsening of accuracy over a session: iMotions recommends extra calibrations for "respondent populations prone to movement," because the mapping learned at the start fits less well once a person has moved, and only a second calibration can show it.
In the simulated data, accuracy averaged 1.71 degrees at the first calibration and 2.42 at the last, and 12 respondents passed the first and failed only the second (all simulated).
Two timing rules follow.
Keep the study "under 10 minutes" (a longer one needs an extra calibration for about every 10 minutes of stimuli).

And show any custom calibration slide for "2 seconds at minimum" (4 is recommended), set in the desktop software before upload: a shorter slide blocks the Start remote data collection button until the cloud study is deleted and uploaded again.
The plan keeps the default animated calibration (how the 2 second rule applies to it is a point to verify).

Its flow, from the Pre-study calibration through Instructions1 (30 seconds), the two videos (60 seconds and 62 seconds), the infographic (15 seconds), and a short survey to the Post-study calibration, took a median of 8.7 minutes with the setup steps (simulated).
Then the losses.

Every session that opens the link passes the respondent funnel, ten steps the portal counts from step 1 Testing upload through step 5 Screen size and step 9 Stimuli presentation* to step 10 Study data upload (the names come from the iMotions Online article; verify that an R D C study shows the same ten).

The funnel is a result to report, not a nuisance: attrition that differs between conditions, selective attrition, is the pitfall named in one study's title, how unattended selective attrition leads to surprising, yet false, research conclusions.
Who opens the link depends on recruitment.

A panel provider recruits and screens respondents, sends them the link, and takes them back at the end through a redirect, an address the study opens when it finishes so that the provider can log the completion and pay; a respondent I D travels in the link's query string, the part after the question mark.
The iMotions article names Forsta, Prolific, Qualtrics, CINT, Amazon mTurk, and Sona Systems.
Prolific's built in integration is not enabled for the lab's account and no other panel account is on record, so class projects send their own links by email.
On what each source brings, read the studies of alternative crowdsourcing platforms, of the data quality of platforms and panels (Peer and colleagues
, 2022) and of MTurk, Prolific, CloudResearch, Qualtrics, and SONA, of Prolific as a subject pool, and of crowdsourcing consumer research.
Nobody watches a remote respondent.

An attention check is a survey item with one correct answer for anyone who read it: one article presents instructional manipulation checks as a way of detecting satisficing, answering with minimal effort, to increase statistical power (Oppenheimer and colleagues

, 2009); another's title reports that MTurk participants performed better on online attention checks than subject pool participants; and careless responding, answering without regard to the content, is the subject of a paper on identifying careless responses in survey data.
A real study should add an attention check to its survey; the simulated study has none, a limitation section 10 names.
Power analysis sets the sample before the data exist.
Power is the probability of detecting an effect of a given size if it is real; the usual target is 80 percent.
For a within subjects comparison the effect size is d z, the mean of the differences divided by their standard deviation.
In plain words.
Comparing two videos within the same people, at alpha point 0 5 and 80 percent power, a large effect (d z equals 0.8) needs 15 kept respondents, a medium one (0.5) 34, and a small one (0.3) 90.
These are respondents left after every loss and exclusion, not people invited.
The same calculation in G*Power Means: difference between two dependent means (matched pairs), two tails, d z equals 0.5, alpha point 0 5, power point 8 0: total sample size 34.
G*Power is the program most researchers cite for this.
A remote study loses many people.
In the simulation, 142 of the 260 sessions that opened a link were kept, 54.6 percent (simulated), so plan for a loss of about 45 percent: divide the kept respondents you need by 0.55 and round up.
For a large effect, 15 divided by 0.55 equals 27.3, so 28 sessions must open the link; the lab's decision guide asks for "60 or more started" in any remote study.
Invitations never opened come on top.
A license may also cap respondents (the lab's Online account began as a 30 respondent trial), so verify the limit on my dot imotions dot com before promising a client a sample.
Devices and homes shape the sample too.
R D C "requires a desktop or laptop computer," and "Participation can not be done on phones or tablets."

On my dot imotions dot com (checked October 12, 2026), the Devices setting of a remote study lists Desktop, Tablet, and Phone, with tablets and phones "Not supported when the study contains stimuli that record the screen"; whether webcam eye tracking works on a tablet or a phone is not stated (verify), so keep a remote eye tracking study to desktop and laptop computers.
R D C supports Chrome, Firefox, Edge, or Safari; iMotions Online names Chrome, Edge, and Firefox.

The invitation asks for even light on the face ("Do not sit in a dark room or with a bright light behind you"), the camera at the top center of the screen, a fixed chair, and no other faces in view, because a respondent on a phone cannot finish and one in front of a bright window risks failing the quality rule.
Consent and privacy are part of the design, not paperwork.
Facial video is identifiable data, and in R D C it goes to iMotions cloud servers and then to the lab computer for post processing.

Informed consent is a documented explanation, given before participation, of the purpose, the right to stop at any time, how the data will be handled, and the risks; for a remote study the consent screen must also say what is recorded, where it is stored and processed, for how long, and who sees it (section 05).
The study first goes to the J S U Institutional Review Board (I R B), the committee that reviews research with human participants, and the lab manual allows cloud upload only with I R B approval.
Minors need a parent's permission and their own assent.

R D C requires acceptance of a Data Processing Agreement (D P A) with iMotions (the text says for E U server users, the portal screen says for every institution; whether J S U has accepted it is not recorded, so verify), and the General Data Protection Regulation (G D P R) applies as soon as E U residents take part.
Background reading covers ethics committees' concerns about online survey tools, ethical considerations and practical guidelines for using Facebook as a research tool (Kosinski and colleagues
, 2015), and the privacy implications of eye tracking.
Last, the exclusion rule, the written condition under which a completed respondent is left out.

The manuals disagree on its threshold: two Online articles say "We recommend a threshold of 3.0" degrees, while the Online study setup guide calls "0 to 4 degrees of visual angle" (degrees of visual angle) the "Generally acceptable range."
The plan uses 4.0 degrees for the rule and 3.0 for a sensitivity analysis, the same tests repeated under the stricter choice.

Eye tracking quality percent is "the ratio of valid eye tracking samples in relation to the total number of samples collected" (at least 90 percent recommended); face quality is the share of samples in which a face was found (at least 80 percent).

The rule: exclude a completed respondent when the Pre-study or the Post-study calibration accuracy is above 4.0 degrees, when eye tracking quality on the infographic is below 90 percent, or when face quality is below 80 percent during either video.
One rule serves every hypothesis, and every exclusion is logged with its reason.

Defend a within subjects design with the order randomized by study flow, size A O I's for a webcam's error, bookend the study with two calibrations, plan the sample with remote losses included, choose a recruitment route, and fix the device rules, consent plan, and exclusion rule before the first link goes out.
The worked example in full
Everything in sections 01 and 02 fits on one page, the first deliverable of any study in this lab.
Below is the remote food waste test as a student study plan; read it as a template for your own.

Among adults who take part at home on their own computers, is the face expressive (aff decks Engagement above 50) for a larger share of the emotional visual video than of the narrative video; does dwell time differ among the four tips of the infographic; and did the order of the videos change the intention to reduce food waste?
H 1: the percent of time Engaged is higher during foodwaste visual than during foodwaste narrative.
H 2: dwell time differs among Tip 1, Tip 2, Tip 3, and Tip 4.
H 3, a randomization check: intention does not differ between the Narrative first and Visual first orders.
Every test can detect a difference in either direction at alpha point 0 5; H 1 is supported only when significant in the predicted direction.
Within subjects for the two videos; the order counterbalanced and assigned by randomization; the infographic and the survey always after both videos, as in the demo.
Study flow 1: foodwaste narrative first.
Study flow 2: foodwaste visual first.

Each study flow has its own collect link, and the invitation list is split at random into two halves, one link each (modeled: verify that an R D C study built in Lab 11 point 1 can hold two flows with a link each).

Pre-study calibration (13 points, 39 seconds), Instructions1 (30 seconds), the two videos in the order of the flow (foodwaste narrative 60 seconds; foodwaste visual 62 seconds), infographic (15 seconds; a headline and four tips to reduce food waste), Questionnaire (an iMotions survey, self paced), Post-study calibration (13 points, 39 seconds).
Under 10 minutes; no image or video larger than 1920 by 1080 pixels.
The default animated 13 point calibrations at the start and the end, both screened by the exclusion rule; no extra calibration, because the stimuli last well under 10 minutes.
Eye tracking (Web Camera) and Respondent camera, chosen when the study is created in iMotions Lab 11 point 1 on the computer with key 0001; they cannot change after upload.

On my dot imotions dot com (lab convention, proposed in the fix checklist): Microphone recording off (no voice task, and the lab has no voice license), no screen recording (no website stimulus), Head position check and Eye detection on, Allow skipping after timeout off, Data upload alternative on with the lab's email address.

Five rectangles, each an area of interest (A O I), on the infographic: Headline, a wide, thin banner (176000 square pixels, 8.49 percent of the screen, about 2.4 degrees tall), and Tip 1 to Tip 4, four equal boxes (262400 square pixels, 12.65 percent each) in reading order from Tip 1 at the top left, with gaps between all five.
Primary: percent of time Engaged (F E A thresholding at 50) for each video; Dwell time (milliseconds) on each tip; Intention reduce food waste 1to7.
Data quality: calibration accuracy at each calibration, eye tracking quality percent on the infographic, face quality during each video, and the session Status.

Described: Joy, Brow Furrow, Positive Valence (+50), Negative Valence (-50), T T F F, and the hit ratio, the percent of respondents with at least one fixation in an A O I (the A O I metric Respondent ratio ( percent)).
Exploratory: More persuasive video and Tips recalled 0to4.
Missing: an attention check (a limitation).

Written before collection: exclude a completed respondent when the Pre-study or the Post-study calibration accuracy is above 4.0 degrees, when eye tracking quality on the infographic is below 90 percent, or when face quality is below 80 percent during either video; log every reason.
Sensitivity analysis: both accuracies at 3.0 degrees or less.

The sessions that entered and stopped at each step of the respondent funnel; the Status counts (Processed, Abandoned, Errors); completion by order; exclusions by reason, by the first criterion failed and by every criterion failed.
Completion and exclusion by order: a chi square test.
Drift: a paired t test of Post-study against Pre-study accuracy.
H 1: a paired t test with d z and its 95 percent confidence interval, checked with a Wilcoxon signed rank test.
H 2: a Friedman test with Kendall's W, then Wilcoxon tests of every pair with Holm's correction.
H 3: Welch's t test with Hedges' g, checked with a Mann Whitney test.
Accuracy and the smallest A O I: a logistic regression of a Headline hit on mean calibration accuracy, reported as an odds ratio per degree.
All tests repeated at 3.0 degrees; exploratory correlations reported as exploratory.

A Personalized consent screen whose text matches the form the I R B approved: the purpose; that the webcam records the face for eye tracking and facial expression analysis, with no screen or microphone recording; that recordings go to iMotions cloud servers and then to the lab computer; how long they are kept and when they are deleted; who sees them; that taking part is voluntary and can stop at any time; and that a respondent I D replaces the name.

A funnel table and figure, a data quality and exclusion table, a table of the tests, four figures, a results section and a discussion in journal form, and a three sentence client summary that says "kept faces more expressive," never "more effective" or "more persuasive."
Several names return in section 08.
A chi square test asks whether completion depends on the order.
The paired t test compares two measures from the same people, and the Wilcoxon signed rank test repeats it on ranks, which matters because percent of time scores pile up at zero.
The Friedman test does this for four measures, Kendall's W (0 to 1) says how consistently respondents rank them, and Holm's correction adjusts p values when several pairs are tested.
Welch's t test compares two groups without assuming equal spread, and the Mann Whitney test repeats it on ranks.
A logistic regression predicts a yes or no outcome, a Headline hit, and its odds ratio says how the odds change with each degree of error.
Each hypothesis has one measure, and H 2 compares only the four equal tip boxes, never the smaller Headline, so that size cannot decide the result.
The quality measures feed the exclusion rule and are reported for everyone who completed.
The real material is the iMotions demo study "(DEMO) Food Waste webET FEA voice" in the Library on the lab computer (Lab Alien).

Captures from October 10, 2026 show a remote study, marked with a cloud icon, with Instructions1 and Instructions2 (30 seconds each), Talkaloud (1 min), Questionnaire (1 min), foodwaste visual (1 min 2 seconds) with three scenes, foodwaste visual Scene[1] to [3], infographic (15 seconds), foodwaste narrative (1 min), and the Pre-study and Post-study calibrations (39 seconds each); four respondents, Respondent 1 to Respondent 4; and, on the Recorded Data tab, Exposure summaries (Calculate) and Affectiva (Post Process).
A visible Calculate button means that the exposure summary, a table of data quality and recorded samples by study, respondent, or stimulus, has not yet been calculated in the lab copy.

The lab's Post Processing menu offers Affectiva for this study, while RealEyes, SpeechToText, audEERING Voice Analysis, Find and blur faces, Body and Hand Pose, Respiration, B alert E E G, and Gaze Mapping are grayed: the lab has no voice module, so the demo's voice results can be viewed but not recomputed.
Its analysis lists the flows aff decks thresholding, aff decks thresholding Aggregation, and Voice Analysis (section 07 shows both screens).
The demo article (versions 10.0 and later) adds the rest.

It pairs a narrative video that explains food waste and steps to reduce it with an emotional one built on "provocative visual imagery," recorded through remote data collection with webcam eye tracking and facial expression analysis, a survey, and a talkaloud task analyzed with voice and speech to text.
Respondents saw both videos, "making this a within-subjects design; the order of the two videos was randomized and the image, survey and talkaloud always followed."
The infographic question was "which of the four steps to reduce food waste was attended to the most."
Its sample analysis thresholded aff decks at 50 and reported engagement during 57 percent of the time for the visual video against 19 percent for the narrative video.
The simulated study points the same way, but with different, simulated people and a different setup, so never compare the two results as if from one study.

Consent, distribution, and collection: from a tested link to the last session
In a lab session a researcher explains the study, watches the setup, and fixes problems.

In a remote study the respondent does all of this alone, guided only by the screens chosen in section 04 and the invitation you write, and decides alone whether to consent, allow the camera, find enough light, and finish.

Because the settings lock at the first respondent, the consent text and a full test come before the real link is shared; once collection runs, your job is to watch where people stop and what quality their data have.
Why.
Informed consent is a person's agreement to take part after being told what will happen.

In a remote study it is given on the consent screen, before anything is recorded, and it covers a face video recorded at home, uploaded to iMotions cloud servers, and, for R D C, downloaded to the lab computer.
Under the lab procedure manual every study needs J S U I R B (Institutional Review Board) approval or exemption "before scheduling participants", and "Any changes, even seemingly minor ones ...
require an I R B amendment."
Remote data always go to the cloud, so the I R B protocol must say so.
Ethics committees have raised their own concerns about research data collected through online tools, and gaze recordings can reveal more about a person than a study needs.
Respondents under 18 need a parent's or guardian's permission and their own assent, obtained as the I R B directs.
The default screens.
The R D C default reads "Welcome!"
and "You have been invited to participate in a study, which will display some media (such as images or videos) while recording your webcam and microphone."
, with the box "I consent to participating in this study and having my face and voice recorded for the duration of the study" and "Accept and continue".
It names face and voice when the microphone is on; the iMotions Online example names the face only.

Neither says where the video goes or for how long, so the lab uses the Personalized consent screen: tick "Use personalized consent text in start screen" on the study's page (section 04) and paste the I R B approved text, which appears "on the very first screen that the participant sees after clicking the link".
It then locks "once the first respondent accepts the consent form".
What the text must say.

The consent F A Q lists "the purpose of the study", "that participation is voluntary", "their rights when participating in the study", "how you will handle the data collected in the study", and "possible risks they may be exposed to during the study", and, for cloud products, "where their data will be stored and processed".

The lab's fix checklist adds that the wording must match what is recorded (face video for both eye tracking and expressions; voice only with the microphone on), that a form "must not say that no video is saved unless iMotions confirms in writing that the recordings are deleted after processing", and that it says who may watch the video.
The lab rule: nobody views a respondent's face unless the consent allows it, and checks are made on numbers (section 07).
Two terms appear in the table.
The Data Processing Agreement (D P A) is the contract under which iMotions processes study data for the university.
The G D P R, the European Union's data protection law, applies "as soon as you have E U residents participating in your study."

The lab rule for these gaps: the consent states only what is confirmed, names the longest retention that may apply and the deletion plan, and matches the I R B protocol; open points are put to iMotions in writing and verified on my dot imotions dot com.
The lab manual gives 7 years for raw physiological data, 5 years for consent forms, and a 3 year example; follow the I R B protocol.

The lab computer is also unlike a respondent's laptop, and browsers and devices differ even in how precisely they time what they show.
Only a test from another computer, through the kind of link a respondent gets, shows what respondents will meet.

A remote study measures with equipment the researcher never sees: the respondent's own webcam, screen, room, and light.
One webcam video gives two signals, an estimate of where the eyes pointed and a record of the face, and the methods section must say how good each was and how it became a number.

This section covers both, what their quality numbers mean for the size of an area of interest (A O I, a region of the stimulus drawn so that gaze inside it can be counted), and what the methods paragraph of a remote study must contain.

Webcam eye tracking finds the eyes in an ordinary webcam image and estimates where on the screen they point; iMotions uses "the iMotions web E T 3.0 algorithm" (Webcam Eye Tracking).

To map one person's eye images to screen positions it needs a calibration: the respondent follows dots at known positions, 13 by default, in a Pre-study calibration at the start and a Post-study calibration at the end.
The lab's Smart Eye Aurora, which you have used if you did Workshop 2 (eye tracking in the lab), lights the eyes with infrared light and is accurate to well under one degree.

The introduction to iMotions Online, the browser based route, says it plainly: "Our webcam eye-tracking algorithm, while powerful, does not have the sub-degree accuracy of a conventional infrared eye tracker," and it "is also sensitive to talking, head movement, and the use of glasses."

A calibration describes the respondent at one moment; then people move, lean back, or the light changes, and the estimate worsens: calibration drift.

R D C studies include both calibrations by default, and the R D C webcam article calls this bookending "currently the best practice that we recommend for webcam eye tracking," with at least 9 points and 4 seconds per calibration slide, plus an extra calibration "for every 10 minutes of study stimuli" (R D C Testing with Webcam Eye Tracking).

In the simulated study accuracy worsened from 1.71 to 2.42 degrees across the 178 completed respondents, and 12 respondents passed the Pre-study calibration but failed the Post-study one: a single calibration at the start would have kept them.

Another 6 with one calibration above 4.0 degrees showed 4.0 or less in the rounded session level "Eye tracking" column of the respondent list (in this simulation the rounded mean of both calibrations; verify what the real column summarizes).
The rule therefore reads each calibration separately (section 08, Figure 4).
An error of a few degrees sets a floor on A O I size.

The iMotions Online introduction advises that "it is best to create large objects that have a buffer of space between them," and the iMotions A O I article cites a recommendation to pad an A O I by about 1 to 1.5 degrees and adds that webcam data need an even greater buffer.
A O I size is exported as Size (px2) and Size ( percent).

In the simulated infographic the four tips are large boxes (12.65 percent of the screen each) separated by gaps, while the Headline is a wide, thin banner (8.49 percent of the screen) about 2.4 degrees tall (Figure 4).
A fixation aimed at its middle falls outside it once the vertical error passes about 1.2 degrees, half its height.
The Headline was fixated by 76.8 percent of the kept respondents against 98.6 to 100 percent for the tips, and the odds of a Headline hit fell with each degree of error (odds ratio 0.61; section 08).
Make A O I's several degrees across, leave gaps, and keep small text out of webcam studies.
A fixation is a pause in which the eyes stay on one spot.

Dwell time (the summed fixation time inside an A O I), time to first fixation (T T F F), and hits are built from fixations, so the filter that groups gaze samples into fixations shapes every A O I number.

The help center names a Hidden Markov Model (H M M) filter, which classifies samples as fixation or movement from the probabilities of switching between those states, as "the default filter for remote data collection studies with webcam-based eye tracking"; iMotions Online labels it "I-H M M filter."
The article also warns that "the typically high levels of noise with low accuracy and precision will not be corrected by any fixation classification filter."

This section runs the planned analyses on the simulated files, in R with analysis dot R (output in analysis output dot T X T) and then in Excel.

The data quality analyses come first, because they decide who is in the tests.

The largest loss was at step 5 Screen size (36 sessions, 34 of them phones or tablets), and none of the 29 phone and 7 tablet sessions completed; in all, 75 sessions (28.8 percent) stopped before the videos, 4 during step 9 Stimuli presentation*, and 3 during the upload (2 abandoned, 1 with errors).

Selective attrition is the danger: if one condition makes more people quit, the finishers differ between conditions, the pitfall of experimenting on the web in which unattended selective attrition leads to surprising (yet false) conclusions.

Each video order was its own study flow, assigned before the link was opened, so Block gives the order of every session, including those that stopped early (modeled: verify that an R D C study built in Lab 11 point 1 can hold two flows with one link each).
A chi square test compares the counts in a table with those expected if order and completion were unrelated; phi (phi) is its effect size, from 0 to 1.

Completion was 87 of 126 sessions (69.0 percent) for Narrative first and 91 of 134 (67.9 percent) for Visual first, chi square(1, N equals 260) equals 0.04, p equals point 8 4 4, phi equals point 0 1.
The sharper check uses the 185 sessions that reached step 9, the first point at which the order could matter: 95.6 against 96.8 percent completed.

Its smallest expected count, 3.44, is below 5, so the Fisher exact test, which computes the probability of the table exactly, is reported: p equals point 7 1 8, odds ratio equals 0.72, 95 percent confidence interval 0.10 to 4.38.
That confidence interval, the range of values compatible with the data, is wide because only 7 sessions were lost after step 9.
Exclusion did not depend on order either, chi square(1, N equals 178) equals 0.02, p equals point 8 8 0 (simulated).
These tests have little power for small differences, so report the counts by order too: a nonsignificant test is not proof of equal attrition.

The exclusion rule, written before collection: exclude a completed respondent when the accuracy of the Pre-study calibration or the Post-study calibration is above 4.0 degrees, when eye tracking quality on the infographic is below 90 percent, or when face quality is below 80 percent during either video.
It removed 36 of the 178 completed respondents (20.2 percent) and kept 142 (69 Narrative first, 73 Visual first).

"First reason" gives each excluded respondent the first criterion failed, in the order of the rule, so it adds up to 36; "failed at all" counts everyone who failed a criterion, so the 14 who failed more than one appear more than once.
In the kept sample, eye tracking quality on the infographic averaged 96.50 percent (standard deviation 2.19), and face quality 96.52 and 96.61 percent during the two videos.

The same 13 point calibration ran at the start and at the end, so a paired t test measures calibration drift: it asks whether the mean of each respondent's difference (Post-study minus Pre-study) is far from zero relative to how much the differences vary.
Its effect size, d z, is the mean difference divided by the standard deviation (standard deviation) of the differences, and the Wilcoxon signed rank test repeats the comparison on ranks.

Accuracy went from M equals 1.71 degrees (standard deviation equals 0.99) to M equals 2.42 degrees (standard deviation equals 1.20), a drift of 0.72 degrees (standard deviation equals 0.50), 95 percent confidence interval 0.64 to 0.79, t(177) equals 19.05, p less than point 0 0 1, d z equals 1.43, 95 percent confidence interval 1.22 to 1.64 (Wilcoxon V equals 15415, p less than point 0 0 1).
Accuracy is an error, so this is a worse estimate at the end, and it was worse for 165 of the 178 respondents (92.7 percent); the two calibrations correlated r equals point 9 1.
Drift was also clear among the 142 kept respondents (0.630 degrees, t(141) equals 16.02), so it belongs to remote data, not only to the people excluded.

The four tips on the infographic are large A O I's.

Dwell time is the summed duration of the fixations inside an A O I (0 milliseconds if it was never fixated, so every respondent counts), time to first fixation (T T F F) is the time from the infographic's onset to the first fixation inside it, and a hit is at least one fixation inside it; the percent of respondents with a hit is the hit ratio, which iMotions calls Respondent ratio ( percent).

Dwell time is skewed, capped by the 15 seconds on screen, and measured four times on the same people, so H 2 uses the Friedman test: within each respondent the tips are ranked from 1 (least dwell) to 4 (most), and the test asks whether the mean ranks differ more than chance allows.

Its effect size, Kendall's W, is the Friedman chi square divided by n (k - 1), where k is the number of tips, and runs from 0 (no agreement among respondents about the order of the tips) to 1 (everyone ranks them the same way).

Mean dwell time was 3742 milliseconds for Tip 1 (standard deviation 1660), 2100 milliseconds for Tip 2 (standard deviation 1421), 2032 milliseconds for Tip 3 (standard deviation 1239), and 2003 milliseconds for Tip 4 (standard deviation 1247), with mean ranks of 3.33, 2.24, 2.27, and 2.16 (Figure 3); Friedman chi square(3) equals 78.95, p less than point 0 0 1, Kendall's W equals point 1 8 5, n equals 142.
Tip 1 had the longest dwell for 83 respondents (58.5 percent).
A significant Friedman test says the tips differ somewhere, not where.

Testing all six pairs with Wilcoxon signed rank tests raises the chance of a false positive, so the p values get the Holm correction: sort them from smallest to largest, multiply the smallest by 6, the next by 5, and so on down to 1, never let an adjusted value fall below the one before it, and cap them at 1.

Tip 1 drew more dwell time than each other tip (mean differences of 1643 to 1739 milliseconds, d z equals 0.66 to 0.73, all Holm p less than point 0 0 1), while Tip 2, Tip 3, and Tip 4 did not differ (mean differences of 29 to 96 milliseconds, all Holm p equals 1.000).
H 2 was supported, with three of the six pairs different.
Nearly everyone fixated every tip (hit ratios of 98.6 to 100 percent), and the median T T F F followed the reading order: 800.5, 2077.5, 3474, and 4206 milliseconds.
Tip 1 sits top left and is read first, so its position and its content are confounded (section 10).
H 3 compares intention to reduce food waste (one item, 1 to 7) between the two orders, which are different people.
Welch's t test compares two independent groups without assuming equal variances, the recommended default (Delacre and colleagues
, 2017), and Hedges' g is the difference in pooled standard deviation units with a small sample correction.

The orders differ only in which video came first, assigned at random, so H 3 is a randomization check: a nonsignificant result is what randomization predicts, and a significant one would mean a chance imbalance or a real order effect.

Intention was M equals 5.04 (standard deviation equals 1.37, n equals 69) after Narrative first and M equals 5.34 (standard deviation equals 1.22, n equals 73) after Visual first, a difference of -0.30, 95 percent confidence interval -0.73 to 0.13, Welch t(135.97) equals -1.37, p equals point 1 7 1, Hedges' g equals -0.23, 95 percent confidence interval -0.56 to 0.10.

The ratings departed from normality (Shapiro Wilk p less than point 0 0 1 in both groups), so the Mann Whitney test, the rank based check for two groups, accompanies it; it agreed, W equals 2243, p equals point 2 4 9.
The result is consistent with H 3 but does not prove the orders equivalent: the interval allows a small difference either way.
